sections.title: 2 Mirror depths and changes of coordinates

html:
A kernel for short solutions of the generalized Rubik’s Cube

Ruimin Yan
(November 26, 2026 Working manuscript)

Abstract

Given a six-colour cube of side n and a budget of k single-layer turns, we give a polynomial-time reduction that either rejects the instance or produces an equivalent cube of the same parity and side at most 4⁢k+7. The output uses at most 6⁢(4⁢k+7)2 stickers. The same reduction works for a prescribed solved colouring and for the goal that each face has one colour and all six colours differ. A lifting argument uses two spare mirror depths to verify every omitted sticker. The reduction, equivalence of the physical instances, and a search bound have been formalized in Lean 4.

1 The decision problem

Each move rotates one layer orthogonal to a coordinate axis by 90∘, −90∘, or 180∘. Each costs one move. The input lists the colours on the six n by n faces in fixed coordinates, with n≥2. Demaine, Eisenstat and Rudoy proved NP-completeness of the unrestricted decision problem [1]. Their colour goal permits any six distinct monochromatic faces. We study the dependence of exact search on the move budget. Direct enumeration already decides the problem in at most ∑i=0k(9⁢n)i candidate words. Its dependence on n motivates reducing the set of candidate layers before searching.

Theorem 1.

Given a legal coloured cube X and an integer k≥0, a polynomial-time algorithm certifies that the distance to the prescribed solved colouring exceeds k, or returns a legal cube Y of side 2≤n′≤4⁢k+7 and of the same parity as n. The original instance satisfies d⁢(X)≤k if and only if d⁢(Y)≤k. The same choice of retained layers preserves solvability within k moves for the goal of six distinctly coloured monochromatic faces.

For example, with n=1000 and k=10, every returned instance has even side at most 46. The decision concerns this particular budget. The argument makes no assertion about equality of distances exceeding it.

2 Mirror depths and changes of coordinates

Number the layers on each axis from 0 through n−1. The two outer layers are distinguished, as is the central layer when n is odd. Group the remaining indices in pairs {i,n−1−i}, called ordinary depths. There are r=⌊(n−2)/2⌋ such pairs. Use the same depth labels on all three axes. A permutation of the r labels acts on the layers of each axis, preserving the side within each pair. A surface sticker has a face and two tangential coordinates. Its support, the set of ordinary depth labels among those coordinates, has size at most two.

A relabelling commutes with coordinate reversal i↦n−1−i. A quarter turn of a layer tests its layer index and exchanges its two tangential coordinates with one reversal. Relabelling therefore carries that turn to the turn on the renamed layer. It fixes the prescribed solved colouring, which depends only on the face. These identities extend to turn words by composition. A word of length at most k names at most k ordinary depths.

Call two depths equivalent for X if their transposition, applied simultaneously on all three axes, preserves every sticker colour of X. This is an equivalence relation. Indeed the stabilizer of X is a group, and conjugating (b⁢c) by (a⁢b) gives (a⁢c) for distinct labels. If a word of length at most k generates X from the prescribed target, all unused depths belong to one class. Swapping any two of them fixes both the word and the solved colouring. Inversion exchanges generating and solving words and preserves length.

3 Reduction and proof

If r≤2⁢k+2, retain all depths. Otherwise find an equivalence class C whose complement has size at most k. If none exists, the unused-depth observation certifies rejection. Keep all of the complement and exactly k+2 members of C. This is possible since r>2⁢k+2. Let R be the retained set. Restrict each face to the surviving rows and columns and renumber the depths consecutively in their original order. Keep both outer layers and the odd central layer.

Lemma 2.

The restricted colouring can be generated from the prescribed target in at most k turns if and only if the original colouring can be generated from its prescribed target in at most k turns.

Proof.

Any word on the original cube projects by omitting turns on removed layers. A retained sticker stays in retained coordinates under every retained turn. A removed-layer turn fixes it. Thus projection preserves the colour read at each retained sticker and cannot increase the length. Projection also preserves legality for an input generated by an arbitrarily long word.

Conversely, embed a short word on the smaller cube by replacing each new depth label with its original label. Call the colouring it produces Z. The turn identities above give Z=X on all retained stickers. If all depths were retained we are done. Otherwise at least two of the k+2 retained members of C are unused by the embedded word. For an omitted sticker choose a distinct spare representative for each omitted depth in its support, avoiding the retained depths already in that support. There are enough spares because the support has size at most two. Swap each omitted label with its chosen representative. Every such swap fixes X by the definition of C, and fixes Z because its labels are unused by the embedded word. Together the swaps carry the sticker to the retained set. Equality at its image proves equality at the original sticker. This proves Z=X everywhere. ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.

There are at most 2⁢k+2 retained depths. With two outer layers and possibly one central layer, the side is at most 2⁢(2⁢k+2)+3=4⁢k+7. The parity is unchanged. Lemma 2 gives both directions. For the monochromatic goal, a completed cube assigns the six colours bijectively to the six faces. A bijection on colours preserves every equality tested by a depth swap. All 6! target assignments consequently use the same retained set. Applying the fixed-target equivalence to each assignment proves the second assertion. ∎

4 Search complexity and verification

With random access to the six colour arrays, the full table testing ordered depth pairs has 6⁢r2⁢n2 colour comparisons. Selecting a class, sorting representatives and materializing the smaller faces take polynomial time in the input size. The smaller cube has 9⁢n′ moves. For a fixed target the search considers at most (9⁢(4⁢k+7)+1)k candidate words, including prefixes. Checking a word against the smaller colouring costs a polynomial in k+1. This yields a fixed-parameter algorithm. Testing all permitted face colours multiplies the search bound by at most 720.

The physical decision theorem is in CubeKernel.Monochrome, the six-array encoding in CubeKernel.Packed, and the search-tree and comparison counts in CubeKernel.Cost. For a prescribed target, the implementation in CubeKernel.Solution returns solving turns with the original layer numbers. The download includes the Lean toolchain and dependency lock. The complexity statement uses the array model above. The checked counts bound comparisons in the complete table and words in the search tree.

Status and assistance.

This working manuscript reports a machine-checked result. The literature comparison does not establish a claim of priority. OpenAI Codex assisted in developing the argument, implementing the Lean proofs and drafting the text.

References

  • [1] E. D. Demaine, S. Eisenstat and M. Rudoy. Solving the Rubik’s Cube optimally is NP-complete. 35th Symposium on Theoretical Aspects of Computer Science, 2018, article 25.
